en: And all the flesh of his soles
Burst and bled upon the stones.
He limped onward in pain,
Leaning against the gray lattice gate;
Külchoro walked with a faltering step,
His power spent and his strength gone.
At twin embankments shaped like a saddle,
He bent forward and stood.
From amid the vast herd,
The bloodthirsty warrior’s gray mare,
That mare taken as plunder,
On seeing Külchoro,
Flung her forelock toward the sky
And stamped her hoof into the ground.
She was a beast once owned by his bloodthirsty uncle;
The pale mare neighed
And circled around him.
The birches wept and the willows wept,
And every living soul who watched them wept.
She had no tongue with which to speak;
As the mare stood there like this,
Your hero Choro wept with her.
The grief burst from his heart;
He burned in anguish and rage,
And despaired of his precious life.
He sobbed in bitter pain,
Abandoning hope of life as though already dead.
When he saw Külchoro,
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Burst into violent rage,
And Külchoro truly
Renounced his fragile life.
He readied himself like a hawk;
What could poor Choro do?
An inspiration came to him as if from the unseen,
And when he saw brave Kyyaz,
Külchoro grew flustered.
The strength drained from his arms,
The courage fled his heart,
His legs hung loose,
His eyes darted wildly,
And he stood stricken with folded hands.
To Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
He humbly offered greeting:
“Peace upon peace be with you,
Noble, illustrious hero Kyyaz!
Your slave has come prepared,
My lord, to plead with you!”
When he saw Külchoro,
He knew his enemy at once,
And Kyyaz, intending to kill him,
Smiled beneath his mustache.
He roared in fury
And spoke to Karagul:
“Ah, Karagul, you wretch!
Why did you not start a bloody fray
With this rabid, cunning slave,
Slaughter him before now,
And finish him for good?
Did I not tell you earlier?
Did he not hear it then?
Without letting them gouge out his glaring eyes,
The pale mare shielded him.
She laid her head upon his shoulder
And stood pressed close to him.
She had no tongue with which to speak,
But showing every sign of love,
The pale mare stood sniffing him.
She has a tail and she has a mane—
Such a creature she is.
Everyone has an animal they cherish.
Oh, dear pale mare,
Rekindle my extinguished fire
And restore my dead soul to life!
She truly was a peerless steed.
That day brave Kyyaz
Appeared upon the hillock.
When enraged, from his mouth
Black flames seemed to pour;
He looked ready to strike down all before him.
His brows were like storm clouds,
And his gaze seemed ready to swallow a soul;
His eyes were like the depths of a lake,
And seeing him, one thought he might devour a man.
His nose was like a jutting ridge,
His force as hard as iron;
He seemed a soul never sated with blood,
A mighty wrestler born to rule a people.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
The fierce Kyyaz, if you saw him,
Was a hulking brute of massive build.
His upturned mustache
Was like a Bukhara saber;
His lower lip sagged wide,
Like a grain merchant’s sack.
His two eyes burned like fire,
Like flames leaping from a hearth;
Such was the appearance
Of grave-devouring Kyyaz.
When he saw Khan Kyyaz,
The lion-born Choro
Lost all strength in his arms.
His knees buckled to the ground,
And as he burned like a glowing ember,
Aichürök came running:
“You burned him before he could burn—
Burn to death yourself, brave Kyyaz!
You cooked him before he was ready—
Be cooked to death yourself, brave Kyyaz!
Would a hero such as you
Lay hands upon slaves and servants?
You lunged about like a madman;
Can anyone rightly call you a hero?
Accursed Kyyaz, may you come to ruin,
May you never find an equal!
Since time immemorial,
You have abused your bondwomen and slaves;
Accursed Kyyaz, you are beyond redemption.
Was this some host gathered by the thousand?
Among your countless people,
Were there no other captive bondwomen or slaves
Except us?
You cooked him before he was ready—
Be cooked to death yourself, Kyyaz!”
Gathering her courage, Aichürök
Shoved mountain-like Kyyaz
And sent him sprawling;
Then she pulled tiny Choro
Out from beneath him.
I thought you mountain-like, Kyyaz,
But you are no larger than a knucklebone!
It seems you are the Kyyaz destined
To see the true abode from which none return!
You shall lie sprawled in the open steppe;
You are the Kyyaz who is to die!
Just you wait, brave Kyyaz!
Because of you, brave Kyyaz,
If I do not don my white-swan plumage,
If I do not soar through the sky,
If I do not destroy you utterly,
If I do not muster my father Akun’s army—
Drawing my bow till arrows rain down—
Why have I not seized and slaughtered him already?
This slave’s appointed death has come;
Now I shall take his head,
Drag him along the road,
And hand him over to the Dangyts!
I shall gouge out his glaring eyes
And slaughter the rabid slave!”
Saying this, brave Kyyaz
Seized his black-edged battle-axe
And swung it around;
He struck down Choro,
The hero favored by fortune.
When mighty Kyyaz struck,
His strength failed and his body weakened,
And brave Choro fell.
Before Khan Kyyaz,
The powerless Choro collapsed;
All his ribs
Were shattered by the blows.
Grunting, Kyyaz kicked him
And tortured Choro.
As brave Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
Was about to show his might,
And was about to cut off
The unconscious Choro’s head,
Aichürök, the lady in the palace,
Heard the newcomers say
That Almambet’s Choro
Was being killed
By Khan Kyyaz before their eyes.
Her heart sank and broke;
Your sister-in-law’s tears poured forth.
From her quail-like eyes,
Tears fell one after another;
From her blackcurrant-dark eyes,
Streams of tears fell a whip’s length.
Unable to stop her running nose,
Unable to wipe away her tears,
She burst into piercing cries
And wailed in bitter anguish.
Brave Kyyaz laughed mockingly,
And now he set aside his anger,
Then Aichürök said:
“Ignorant Kyyaz, hear my words!
No racehorse has flawless hooves,
No falcon has flawless wings.
If you carry on like this, Kyyaz,
If I do not flood your home,
Just wait, accursed Kyyaz—
If I live, one day I shall bring you down!
When costly crimson cloth
Is torn at the hem, it does not unravel;
Once you fall into Kyrgyz hands,
You will not even dare look back.
If my father Akun has no means,
If I do not pursue you and prove my words,
If I do not soar thunderously, seeking warriors,
If I do not range across the earth,
If I do not gather men from passes
High as towering cliffs,
If I do not gather lions
Who have subdued the whole wide world—
Was your heart not content, taking captives,
Humiliating them and gathering slaves?
Had you no other maidservant or slave but us?
Since time beyond remembering,
You have barred your way with iron,
Slaughtered nations in your wrath—
Why have you subjected us to such disgrace?
You smirk and fawn, brave Kyyaz;
Can good come to one who strikes a slave?
You have done the vilest of all deeds for a warrior;
Can a hero truly be like you?”
With a handspan waist and moonlike face,
Your renowned sister-in-law Chürök
Showed her heroic mettle;
She separated him from Kyyaz
And brought the helpless Choro
Inside the white pavilion.
“When I enter the white pavilion,
If I do not shoot arrows like hail
And utterly destroy your host!
If I do not cast your troops into hell,
If I do not take my vengeance without pause,
If I do not bring slaughter upon your borders,
If I do not cut off your head with my sword!
If I do not reap your green grain,
If I do not ravage your entire village!
If I do not rally my father Khan Akun’s army,
Make bows rain like a storm,
And arrows fall like hail—
Should you die, brave Kyyaz,
If I do not unleash open war
And slaughter your settled people!
If I do not bring calamity upon your head,
Whatever your last wish, brave Kyyaz,
If I do not exact my vengeance upon you!
If I do not summon Akun’s people
And have your giant bound,
I shall draw out, brave Kyyaz,
All your long-stored bitterness!”
Chürök, daughter of Akun,
The moon-faced woman of tumult,
A champion among women,
A heroic tigress,
Your fierce and precious sister-in-law—
Can any woman surpass her?
Such was your fierce sister-in-law;
Can any female surpass her?
When brave Kyyaz heard this,
His very ribs quaked.
“A woman will do what she threatens,” he thought,
“She may do all manner of things.”
Then Kyyaz said:
